description:
The AI is not the bottleneck. The joint is.

A humanoid robot is, mechanically, a collection of actuators with a computer attached. Between 28 and 44 of them decide what the machine can lift, how long it runs, and what it costs to build — and they carry 40 to 60 per cent of the bill of materials.

The industry has split into two physical actuation species, and neither has won outright: rotary drivetrains own the arms and torso, linear roller screws own the payload leg. Chinese vendors took all six top places in 2025 humanoid shipments — and that lead is an actuation-cost outcome, not an actuation-performance one.

This humanoid actuation report takes the joint apart layer by layer: the physics that sets the limits, the five competing transmission architectures, the component vendors behind every major platform, and the five cost curves that gate adoption to 2036.

Inside the report

  • 249 pages, ~99,000 words — executive summary, 15 chapters and an appendix
  • 49 tables, 24 figures, 625 primary sources — filings, prospectuses, patents, datasheets and teardowns, ahead of press summaries
  • Thirty humanoid platforms compared in one architecture matrix, West and China side by side
  • A 75-supplier directory with an explicit exposure tier against every name
  • Tesla Optimus reconstructed from the primary record, including the arithmetic on the target price everyone quotes
  • Ten-year outlook to 2036 where every prediction carries a dated trigger indicator that would falsify it
  • Every figure carries its confidence tier; where credible sources disagree, both are reported

Scope

Motors, gearing, linear actuation, dexterous hands, drive electronics and the actuator supply chain, 2026–2036.

Written for

Joint and actuator engineers · component vendors deciding where to place capacity · OEM procurement and supplier qualification · Tier 1 integrators · bearing, encoder, screw and drive suppliers · corporate strategy, M&A, and investor teams.

PDF, delivered immediately. Free updates throughout the 2026 cycle. Just released – August 2026.

name: Booster T2
short_description: Booster T2 is Booster Robotics’ flagship embodied-AI development platform, built for researchers and developers who need strong compute, agile motion, and configurable end effectors.
description:
Booster T2 comes from Booster Robotics, a Chinese robotics company known for its earlier T1 platform. The T2 serves as the company’s new flagship, built for developers and researchers who want a serious embodied AI platform. It brings stronger compute, added sensors, and more advanced movement than its predecessor. As a result, teams can push further into perception, manipulation, and real-world task execution.

The robot senses its surroundings through cameras placed in its head and waist, so it builds a clear picture of the space around it. It doesn’t just observe that space; it interprets it and reacts in real time. This lets the T2 handle scenarios that shift and change, rather than following a fixed script. Meanwhile, its onboard compute keeps that response loop fast and consistent.

Booster built the T2 to handle real physical work, not just demonstrations. Its arms carry meaningful payload, and its joints use industrial-grade bearings for durability. Depending on the configuration, it uses either a simple gripper or a fully dexterous hand for finer manipulation. Therefore, the T2 can move from basic pick-and-place work to more delicate, hands-on tasks.

Developers can shape the T2 into almost any project through Booster’s open software tools. The platform connects to Booster Studio, an agent store, and open-source resources, so teams can build and test new skills quickly. Booster also designed the T2 for demanding, competitive environments like RoboCup. Consequently, it works equally well in a research lab and on a competition field.

name: H2 Plus
short_description: The Unitree H2 Plus is a 1.82-meter, 70-kilogram research humanoid robot built for frontier AI and robotics R&D. It serves as the official hardware body of NVIDIA’s first Isaac GR00T Reference Humanoid, bundling Unitree’s full-stack mechanics with NVIDIA Jetson Thor on-board compute, optional Sharpa Wave five-finger tactile hands, and the open Isaac GR00T software stack. Ships globally in late 2026.
description:
Unitree built the H2 Plus as a full-stack humanoid platform for advanced research and development. Moreover, the Chinese company integrated nearly everything in-house — joint motors, bearings, body materials, and onboard compute. Then NVIDIA selected this exact robot as the body for its first open Isaac GR00T reference design. As a result, the H2 Plus arrives bundled with Jetson Thor compute, Sharpa Wave hands, and Isaac GR00T software. Researchers and developers get a single integrated package rather than a parts-bin assembly.

The robot stands 1.82 meters tall and weighs about 70 kilograms with its battery. Inside, Unitree uses low-inertia inner-rotor permanent magnet synchronous motors and industrial-grade crossed roller bearings for joint motion. The body itself combines aerospace-grade aluminum, titanium alloy, and high-strength engineering plastics. Therefore, the H2 Plus handles heavy loads without becoming clumsy. Each arm produces peak torque of 120 N·m and lifts up to 15 kilograms at peak. Meanwhile, each leg drives 360 N·m of peak torque for dynamic walking and balance.

Two Intel x86 PCs handle the base platform and user development out of the box. However, the real power comes from the optional NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000 module. That single chip delivers 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of AI performance through a 2560-core Blackwell GPU. In addition, a 14-core Arm Neoverse V3AE CPU and 128 GB of unified memory back it up. For vision, the robot uses a 5 MP head-mounted stereo camera with a 140° horizontal field of view. Optional 3 MP wrist cameras add ultra-wide 196° peripheral coverage for close-range manipulation. Beyond compute, the robot also covers Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.2, Gigabit Ethernet, and USB, GMSL, and CAN interfaces.

The optional Sharpa Wave dexterous hands push total degrees of freedom to 75 across the body. Each five-finger hand carries 22 active DOF and over 1,000 tactile pixels per fingertip. Additionally, pressure sensitivity reaches 0.005 N, which lets the robot feel very fine contact. On top of the hardware, NVIDIA’s open Isaac GR00T platform runs simulation, training, evaluation, and deployment workflows. Importantly, researchers retain ownership of their robot data, training data, and logs throughout the process. Unitree begins shipping the H2 Plus globally in late 2026. In addition, each unit comes with a 12-month warranty and full secondary-development support.
